hints: Focus on what is left behind and what escapes as gas, since only the solid oxide remains after strong heating.
Write the decomposition equations for a Group 2 carbonate and a Group 2 nitrate, then work out the Mr of each of the four starting solids.
Calculate percentage loss as (mass of gases lost / Mr of starting compound) x 100, and see which combination of light metal plus large gas loss wins.
walkthrough:
**Recall the decomposition reactions**

Great start, let's remember what happens on heating. Carbonates lose only carbon dioxide, while Group 2 nitrates lose nitrogen dioxide and oxygen.

$$\text{MCO}_3 \rightarrow \text{MO} + \text{CO}_2$$
$$2\text{M}(\text{NO}_3)_2 \rightarrow 2\text{MO} + 4\text{NO}_2 + \text{O}_2$$

**Find the mass lost per mole**

The solid oxide stays, the gases are lost. So mass lost is the mass of the gases.

For carbonates: loss = $M_r(\text{CO}_2) = 44.0$

For nitrates (per 1 mole): loss = $4 \times M_r(\text{NO}_2) + M_r(\text{O}_2)$ divided by 2 $= (4 \times 46.0 + 32.0)/2 = 108.0$

**Calculate percentage loss for each compound**

Percentage loss = (mass lost / $M_r$ of starting compound) x 100. A smaller $M_r$ with a large gas loss gives a bigger percentage.

$$\text{CaCO}_3: M_r = 100.1, \% = 44.0/100.1 \times 100 = 44.0\%$$
$$\text{Ca}(\text{NO}_3)_2: M_r = 164.1, \% = 108.0/164.1 \times 100 = 65.8\%$$
$$\text{MgCO}_3: M_r = 84.3, \% = 44.0/84.3 \times 100 = 52.2\%$$
$$\text{Mg}(\text{NO}_3)_2: M_r = 148.3, \% = 108.0/148.3 \times 100 = 72.8\%$$

**Pick the greatest loss**

Well done, now just compare. Magnesium nitrate has the lightest metal with the heaviest gas loss, so it gives the highest percentage at about 73%. That is the greatest loss.

options.A: Incorrect. $\text{CaCO}_3 \rightarrow \text{CaO} + \text{CO}_2$ loses only 44.0 out of 100.1, about 44%. Calcium is heavy and only one $\text{CO}_2$ is lost, so this is the smallest loss.
options.B: Incorrect. $\text{Ca}(\text{NO}_3)_2$ loses 108.0 out of 164.1, about 66%. Although nitrates lose more gas mass than carbonates, the heavy calcium makes the percentage lower than for magnesium nitrate.
options.C: Incorrect. $\text{MgCO}_3 \rightarrow \text{MgO} + \text{CO}_2$ loses 44.0 out of 84.3, about 52%. The lighter magnesium helps, but losing only $\text{CO}_2$ gives less loss than losing $\text{NO}_2 + \text{O}_2$.
options.D: Correct. $2\text{Mg}(\text{NO}_3)_2 \rightarrow 2\text{MgO} + 4\text{NO}_2 + \text{O}_2$ loses 108.0 out of 148.3, about 73%. This combines the lightest cation ($\text{Mg}^{2+}$) with the largest mass of gaseous products, giving the greatest percentage loss.
